blocks.text: The most stable scale. The seventh degree does the work — it sits a semitone below the root and wants to resolve upward, which is where major's brightness and sense of home come from.
Watch the fourth. Over a major chord it is an **avoid note**: fine passing through, but land on it and the chord's colour goes muddy. If you want that sound, use Lydian's #4 instead.

items: Safest over: Imaj7 and IVmaj7
Genres: the backbone of pop, country and gospel

blocks.text: The minor third makes it minor, but the sixth is **major** — one shade less melancholy than natural minor, and considerably more groove. This is the default minor of funk and soul.
The **6** is the signature note. Lean on it and Dorian announces itself; avoid it and you have slid back into natural minor.

items: Typical setting: a long vamp on one m7 chord (Dm7 repeating)
Genres: funk, soul, Latin rock, modal jazz

scale.phrygian.title: Phrygian: a semitone out of the gate

blocks.text: **b2** sits immediately above the root, so the scale opens with downward semitone pressure. Nearly all of its Spanish and Middle Eastern colour comes from that one note.
The b2 is both signature and centre of gravity. Treating it as a passing note wastes it — put it on a strong beat and the character holds.

items: Genres: flamenco, metal riffs, film cues reaching for 'the East'

blocks.text: Major with the fourth raised to **#4**. Without Ionian's avoid note, every tone is safe to sit on, and the scale reads as floating up rather than resolving down.
On a chart it appears as **maj7#11**. For the clearest example, listen to any film cue scoring 'vast' or 'wondrous'.

items: Genres: film scores, fusion, the bright passages of city pop

scale.mixolydian.title: Mixolydian: home of the dominant chord

blocks.text: A major third with a **b7** — exactly the notes of a dominant seventh. Bright, but with no leading tone it is in no hurry to resolve, so it can stay put indefinitely.
Any section parked on a 7 chord — the I7 of a blues, a funk E9 vamp — reaches for this first.

items: Genres: blues rock, funk, Celtic music

blocks.text: Three flats — b3, b6, b7 — and the standard sound of melancholy. It is the sixth mode of its relative major: A minor uses exactly the notes of C major, and the only difference is which note you treat as home.

One practical catch: the fifth degree of Aeolian is a **minor chord** (Em in A minor), which cannot push a strong resolution. For the force of E7 to Am you must raise the b7 to 7 — that is, borrow from harmonic minor.

items: Genres: rock ballads, minor-key folk, game soundtracks

scale.locrian.title: Locrian: a root that will not stand

blocks.text: **b5** turns the tonic chord into m7b5 — a chord that cannot settle. That is why the scale is almost never used as a key centre.
Its real job is as a **chord scale**: the iim7b5 in a minor 2-5-1 (Bm7b5 in A minor) is Locrian. Rather than memorising it as a mode, tie it to the m7b5 chord.

items: Where you meet it: the first chord of a minor ii-V-i

scale.majorPentatonic.title: Major pentatonic: major with the friction removed

blocks.text: Take the major scale and drop **4** and **7**. Those two are precisely the notes most likely to clash — the 4 is an avoid note over I, and the 7 grinds a semitone against IV.

With the explosives removed, you can play anything over a whole major progression and not be wrong — hence the safety net. The cost is that the character left with them: to get flavour back, you have to add notes back.

items: How to use it: shape the melody with the pentatonic, then add 4 or 7 for tension

scale.minorPentatonic.title: Minor pentatonic: the mother tongue of rock

blocks.text: Natural minor without **2** and **b6**. The starting point of nearly every rock solo, and the first shape most guitarists commit to memory.

Worth internalising: it is the **same set of notes** as the major pentatonic of the relative major (A minor pentatonic = C major pentatonic). One shape, two sounds — which note you treat as home decides which one you hear.

items: Next step: add b5 for the blues scale, add 6 for a Dorian flavour

scale.blues.title: Blues scale: the one extra note

blocks.text: Minor pentatonic plus **b5** — a single note's difference. That note is the blue note, and nearly all of the blues' tension rides on it.
It is a **passing note, not a resting note**. Slide up from the 4 or down from the 5 and it sings; stop on it and the tension is severe — unless severe is what you came for.

items: Drill it: 4 to b5 to 5 and back, connected with bends or slides

scale.harmonicMinor.title: Harmonic minor: all for the leading tone

blocks.text: Natural minor with the b7 raised to **7**. The purpose is simple: give minor a leading tone, which turns the fifth degree into a true V7 (E7 in A minor) so the resolution home actually lands.
The side effect became the signature — the gap from b6 to 7 is an **augmented second**, three semitones. That unusual leap is where the exotic colour comes from.

items: Genres: classical minor, neo-classical metal, Eastern European and Middle Eastern styles
Practical entry point: switch to harmonic minor only for the V7 bar, natural minor everywhere else

blocks.text: A minor third, but major sixth and seventh — easiest understood as **the major scale with a flattened third**.
Classical harmony uses it ascending only, reverting to natural minor on the way down. Jazz uses it in both directions, which is why it is also called **jazz minor**.
Its value is as a parent scale: many modern scales are its modes, and the seventh of them is the **altered scale**, used over V7alt.

items: Chord match: m(maj7), and the minor colour of fusion and neo-soul

blocks.text: The lit notes on the fretboard are a map. Practice turns the map into muscle. This order works better than memorising shapes first.

items: **Along one string first**: run the scale from lowest to highest on a single string. This stage teaches your ear the distances, not your fingers the shape.
**Then across the neck**: hold one position and run all six strings up and down. Now you are learning the shape.
**Finally, connect**: shift between two positions. Put the shift on a weak beat or across a bar line so the pulse never breaks.

blocks.text: Using the click: start at a tempo you can play **completely clean**, and add 5 only after three flawless passes. A tempo you stumble at is not your tempo.

ii–V–I is the strongest resolution formula in tonal music: ii sets it up, V builds tension, I resolves. Adding vi keeps the phrase from truly stopping and sends it back to the top — hence **turnaround**.
Why so strong? The roots move in **descending fifths**: D to G to C to A. That is exactly the counterclockwise direction of the circle, and the harmonic gravity the ear knows best.

items: Listen: Autumn Leaves, Fly Me to the Moon — nearly any standard
Focus: move as few fingers as possible between chords; find the common tones

blocks.text: It opens on IV rather than I, so it hangs in mid-air from the first bar and only lands on I at the very end. That float-then-land shape is the signature of Japanese pop and city pop.
The **iii–vi** in the middle darkens a bright major key, then ii–V–I reels it all back in. The emotional arc is written into the chords; the melody only has to follow.

items: Also known as: the royal road progression
Focus: the seventh-chord version carries far more of the flavour than triads

blocks.text: I–vi–IV–V. So common in 1950s doo-wop that it is simply called the **doo-wop changes**. Stand by Me is the easiest example to hear.
It works for a plain reason: all four chords are the most stable members of the key, vi supplies a touch of shadow, and V guarantees you want to go around again every four bars.

items: Focus: the first loop a beginner should own — get changes automatic

blocks.text: vi–IV–I–V is 1645 started from a different point. Beginning on the minor makes it a shade sadder, then arriving at I lifts it again.
Two decades of pop leaned on it hard enough to earn the 'four chord song' joke. That is not laziness — the emotional arc is simply that useful.

items: Focus: same four chords, different voicings — see how much mood you can change

progression.canon.title: Canon progression: the bass is walking

blocks.text: I–V–vi–iii–IV–I–IV–V, from Pachelbel's Canon. The point is not the chords but the **stepwise descending bass**: C–B–A–G–F–C–F–G.
The bass walks smoothly and the chords above are dragged along behind it — a textbook case of harmony being decided by a line.

items: Focus: sing the root while you play and feel that descent

progression.blues12.title: 12-bar blues: a whole song on three chords

blocks.text: I7, IV7 and V7 laid into a fixed 12-bar grid. What makes it unusual is that **all three are dominant sevenths** — in classical harmony that is 'wrong', because a dominant is supposed to resolve.
The blues simply refuses to resolve it and leaves it hanging. That unresolved quality is the sound of the blues itself.

items: Quick change: touch IV7 in bar 2 so the opening is less static
Focus: get the 12-bar length into your body before you worry about soloing

chord.borrowed-iv.title: Why can C major borrow Fm?

blocks.text: Fm is not in C major — the fourth degree there is F major. Yet it sounds not merely acceptable but especially good. The reason is **modal interchange**: borrowing a chord from the parallel minor.

In C minor the fourth degree is exactly Fm (F–Ab–C). What the borrowing adds is the **Ab**, the b6 of C. That is the whole trick: a semitone below the major's A, it creates the descent **Ab to G**, landing straight on the fifth of C.
So the ache of Fm comes from that semitone, not from minor-ness. Voice the Ab on top and let it fall to G — the effect is unmistakable.

items: Typical use: I – iv – I, the minor four as a sigh before coming home
The same logic borrows bVII, bVI and bIII, all from the parallel minor
Listen: the Beatles, Radiohead, and nearly every city pop turnaround

chord.secondary-dominant.title: Secondary dominants: treating another note as home

blocks.text: V/ii reads as 'the five of the two'. In C major, ii is Dm, and the dominant of D is A7. So A7 to Dm is a miniature resolution, even though A7 does not belong to C major (it contains C#).

The effect is to treat Dm as a temporary tonic, adding a push the diatonic chords cannot. Because each secondary dominant resolves down a fifth, chaining them produces a **descending-fifths run**: E7–A7–D7–G7–C.

items: Most used: V/ii (A7), V/V (D7), V/vi (E7)
How to spot one: an out-of-key major third (C# in C) usually means a secondary dominant

chord.bVII.title: bVII: the flat seven of rock

blocks.text: In C major, a Bb major triad. It is borrowed too — from C Mixolydian, or equally from the parallel minor. Without the leading tone B, the way home stops being a resolution and becomes a slide.
That is precisely what rock and funk want: force without formality. I–bVII–IV–I is the skeleton of countless riffs.

items: Listen: Sweet Home Alabama and most of seventies rock
It is the same fact as the Mixolydian scale, stated as a chord

chord.blues-dominants.title: Why all-dominant blues is not a mistake

blocks.text: In classical harmony a dominant seventh must resolve to the tonic. The blues makes I a dominant too, leaving the whole song suspended.

This is not misuse but a different system: the tension comes from the **blue notes** in the melody (b3, b5, b7) grinding against major-third chords. A dominant seventh happens to hold a major third and a minor seventh at once, so it became the default blues chord.

items: In practice: solo with minor pentatonic or blues scale over dominant backing — the friction is the point

blocks.text: Swap triads for **maj9, m9 and m11** and the sound goes from clean to airy. The added 9th sits a major second from the root, and that small friction is where the laid-back quality comes from.
The other move is **parallel motion**: hold one voicing shape and slide the whole thing, whether or not the destination is strictly in key. Brief excursions outside let the harmony breathe.

items: Starting point: Imaj9 – vim9 – iim9 – V7, played slowly so the extensions are heard
Voicing tip: drop the fifth and keep root, third, seventh and ninth

rhythm.subdivisionGrid.title: The grid: rhythm is really only one thing

blocks.text: Every rhythm is a variation on the same idea: **cut the beat into slots, then decide which slots sound**. Quarters give one slot, eighths two, sixteenths four. Syncopation, dotted notes and swing are all built on that grid.
Practising rhythm is not memorising patterns, it is teaching the hand **where each slot lives**. Once the grid is internalised, you can play anything you can read.

items: Keep the strumming hand moving up and down at all times — silent slots still get an air stroke. If the hand stops, the grid breaks.
Accurate before fast: a rhythm you cannot play slowly will only fall apart faster.

blocks.text: Downbeats (1 2 3 4) are easy against a click. Offbeats (&) are hard, because **there is no click to lean on**. The offbeat drill removes the downbeat click entirely and sounds only the &, forcing you to hold the grid yourself.
You will speed up or drag at first — that is normal. Hold eight bars without drifting and your time has moved up a level.

items: Count '1 & 2 &' internally, but only play the &
Keep tapping the downbeat with your foot: the body needs a silent reference
If you cannot hold it, drop to 60 BPM. Slow and certain beats fast and guessed.

rhythm.sixteenthPositions.title: 1 e & a: the four sixteenth-note slots

blocks.text: Four slots per beat, counted **1 e & a**. Each has a character: the downbeat is the anchor, the **&** is the half-beat (the eighth-note offbeat), and **e** and **a** exist only once you subdivide into sixteenths.
Most 'my sixteenths are sloppy' problems are not about hand speed — they are about not distinguishing e from a. So drill them apart: a whole passage on the e, then a whole passage on the a.

items: The e sits just after the downbeat and sounds like a rush
The a sits just before the next downbeat and sounds like a push — most of funk's forward drive comes from here
The hand keeps its sixteenth-note motion throughout; all that changes is which slot touches the strings

rhythm.syncopation.title: Syncopation: accents leave the whole-number slots

blocks.text: **Syncopation** means putting the accent where one does not belong. The dotted eighth and the tresillo are the ancestors of them all; learn those two and you can take apart nine tenths of popular music.

A **dotted eighth** lasts one and a half eighths. Played in a row, the accent lands every 3 slots against a 4-slot beat, creating a 3-against-4 tension that only resolves back onto the downbeat after three bars.
The **tresillo (3-3-2)** is the skeleton of Latin and modern pop: sixteen slots grouped 3+3+2. It sounds like reggaeton, like Despacito, like half of K-pop.

items: Count slots, not vibes: 3-3-2 means slots 1, 4 and 7
Ties across the bar line are where the pulse usually breaks — leave the click on and let it count for you

rhythm.ghostNote.title: Ghost notes: barely audible, badly missed

blocks.text: A **ghost note** is what you get when the fretting hand relaxes its pressure and the strumming hand strikes anyway — a muted 'chk' with almost no pitch and very little volume. It is what holds the sixteenth-note grid together.
Strip every ghost note out of a funk part and the accents become isolated dots: dry, stiff, no groove. Ghosts are not decoration, they are **the floor the rhythm stands on**.

items: Rest the fretting hand lightly on the strings, without pressing to the fret; the strumming motion is unchanged
The demo click here models ghosts with a low frequency plus a lowpass filter, so they read as dull rather than merely quiet
Try strumming nothing but ghosts first, until the hand stops stalling

rhythm.funkGrid.title: Why funk locks to the sixteenth grid

blocks.text: In funk the strumming hand is a metronome: **the sixteenth-note motion never stops**. What changes is which slot touches the strings, which is an air stroke, and which is a ghost. The moment the hand stops to wait for the next accent, the time falls apart.

James Brown's '**on the one**' is about putting the accent back on beat one. Rock puts its weight on 2 and 4; funk puts the biggest hit back on 1, so the whole band aligns there and the remaining fifteen slots have something to push against.

items: Drill the motion and the ghosts first, then place the accents into the grid
If it is not clean, lower the BPM — do not switch to eighths, that is a different genre

rhythm.backbeat.title: The backbeat: that hit on 2 and 4

blocks.text: The **backbeat** puts the accent on beats 2 and 4. It is the shared skeleton of rock, soul and R&B — the snare lands there, and so does the audience's clapping.

What makes soul and R&B subtle is **give and take**: a backbeat placed a hair late feels relaxed (laid back), a hair early feels urgent. That is feel, not error — but you have to be able to hit it dead-on before you have earned the right to push it around.

items: Nail 2 and 4 against the click first, then try landing about 10 ms late and hear the difference
How hard you hit the offbeats decides how sticky the groove feels

blocks.text: Both delay the second half of the beat; they differ in **degree and context**. Straight puts the offbeat at 50% (dead centre); a full shuffle puts it at **2/3** — the third slot of a triplet, conventionally called 66% (exactly 66.7%).

**Shuffle** usually means the explicit, bouncing triplet feel of the blues, close to the maximum. **Swing** is the jazz term and its degree floats: slow tunes sit near a full shuffle, fast tunes drift back towards straight.

items: 50% straight, around 58% for a light swing (where a lot of pop actually sits), 66.7% for a full shuffle
Push one pattern from 50 to 67 and hear it turn into a different genre
Triplet subdivision already sits where a full shuffle lands, so triplets take no swing

blocks.text: Both hold six eighth notes per bar; the difference is **grouping**. 3/4 is three big beats of two (1-2 3-4 5-6, three groups of two); 6/8 is two big beats of three (1-2-3 4-5-6, two groups of three).
So 6/8 accents **1 and 4** and walks with a rocking two; 3/4 accents 1, 3 and 5 and turns into a waltz. Same six notes, completely different direction.

items: Slow blues and gospel mostly live in 6/8 or 12/8 (four big beats of three)
Here a 'beat' is the time signature's lower number, so a 6/8 BPM counts eighth notes
Start on the two-big-beat feel to get the body moving, then switch to the six-small-beat feel to count slots
